title: Lean prompt: turn raw Gemba walk notes into a prioritised action list with owner roles and due dates
summary: Paste unedited notes from a shopfloor or hangar walk. Copilot separates what was seen from what was assumed, tags SQDC and waste, and drafts actions with owner roles, dates and a way to verify.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a lean coach with long Gemba experience in [machining / assembly / composite shop / MRO hangar]. You separate what was seen from what was assumed, and you never turn a person into the cause of a problem.

Context: I walked [area, line or hangar bay] on [date] from [start time] to [end time] with [roles only, no names]. Focus of the walk: [safety / flow / 5S / standard work / quality at source]. Below are my raw notes, unedited, in the order I wrote them. Site rules: safety items always rank first; every action needs an owner ROLE (not a person's name, unless I give one); due dates are within [10] working days unless a reason is given.

Notes:
[paste notes here]

Task:
1. Split the notes into three lists: Observations (seen, measured or heard, ideally with a number; if there is no number write "no number"), Interpretations (conclusions I or someone else drew), and Questions for the next walk.
2. Tag every observation with S, Q, D, C or P (Safety, Quality, Delivery, Cost, People) and, where it clearly fits, one of the eight wastes (Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilised talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra processing).
3. Escalate now: list any observation that could mean an immediate injury risk, an unidentified or unmarked part, a tool or gauge out of calibration, or a possible quality escape. For these write only "Escalate to [safety officer / quality] per our procedure" and what was seen. Do not propose a fix for them.
4. Action list, only for observations with enough evidence. Table columns: ID, Action (verb first), Linked observation, Owner role, Due date, Effort (S/M/L), Expected effect, How we verify.
5. Needs more facts: items where evidence is thin, each with the one question to ask and the role to ask.
6. Three questions to ask on the next walk of the same area.

Format: Tables where I asked for columns, short bullets elsewhere. Maximum two pages.

Rules: Use only my notes. Do not invent measurements, counts or times. If a note describes a person's behaviour, restate it as a process condition (for example "no clear place for the gauge" instead of "operator is careless") and add the flag "People item, route via line manager".
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented notes: "Cell 4, 07:40. Two pallets of finished brackets in the walkway at the door, about 1 m from the red line. Operator walks to the tool crib for the same deburring tool 3 times in 20 min. Whiteboard shows target 120 parts, actual 74 at 09:30 - nobody could say why. Gauge on bench 2 has no calibration sticker. Coolant smell stronger than last week. Setup sheet on the machine is dated 2019."

What a good answer contains:
- Observations: pallets near the walkway (Safety, Transportation/Inventory), 3 walks in 20 minutes to the crib (Motion, count given), 74 of 120 at 09:30 (Delivery, reason unknown), gauge without sticker, coolant smell (no number), setup sheet dated 2019.
- Escalate now: the gauge without calibration sticker (quality process decides whether parts measured with it need a check) and the pallets near the walkway if your rules treat that as a safety issue.
- Actions with owner roles: "Move the deburring tool to a point-of-use shadow board at cell 4" (Team leader, 10 days, effort S, verify by counting crib trips in a 20-minute observation); "Check the setup sheet against current practice and reissue" (Process engineer).
- Needs more facts: why 74 of 120 (arithmetic from the notes: 62 percent of target, which Copilot may show only because both numbers are in the notes).
- Next-walk questions: "What stopped the cell between 08:00 and 09:30?" and similar.

WHEN TO USE
After a Gemba walk, a safety tour or a layered process audit, while the details are still fresh (same day). It also helps when several managers each did a walk and you want one combined list. It does not replace the walk: the value is in standing at the place, and the prompt only structures what you saw.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- Raw notes, however messy (typed, dictated on the phone, or a photo transcribed into text).
- Walk focus, date, area, roles of the people who came.
- Your site's rules for safety escalation, owner roles and due dates, if they differ from the defaults.
- Optional: the SQDC targets of the area, so observations can be compared to them.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Three lists (observations, interpretations, questions), an escalate-now block, an action table with owner roles and verification, a list of open facts and three questions for the next walk. Read it with the notes beside you and strike every line you cannot trace back.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Pasting only the tidied version. The raw order often shows what you noticed first, and tidying removes the numbers.
- Accepting actions for observations that have no number. Ask for the measurement first.
- Letting the action list grow to 25 items. Keep the top 5 to 7 and say what you will not do.
- Treating the Copilot tagging as final. Waste tags are a conversation starter for the team, not a finding.
- Posting names next to problems. Use roles, and keep behaviour topics with the line manager.

HOW TO ADAPT
Change the focus line to match the walk type (for example "5S only" or "material flow only"). For a layered process audit, replace the waste tags with the audit questions of your checklist. For an MRO hangar, add the headings tooling control, foreign object damage prevention and documentation at the aircraft. For a recurring walk, paste last week's action list and add the task "Mark which earlier actions look closed, still open or contradicted by this week's notes". Ask for a version for the SQDC board with only five lines if the whole list is too long.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Notes often contain names, shift patterns and remarks about individual behaviour. Anonymise them before pasting and use roles. If the walk includes any performance remarks about individuals, involve HR and the works council or data protection officer before using AI on such notes, in line with your agreements. Do not paste customer drawings, export-controlled technical data or anything marked for restricted distribution unless your security rules allow it. Safety and quality escalations follow your own procedures; Copilot only helps you notice and word them.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. title: Lean prompt: find the eight wastes in a written process description and rank them by effect on lead time
summary: Turn a written walk-through of a process into a step table with value-adding, required and waste steps, a calculated flow efficiency, the top five wastes ranked and countermeasure ideas to verify at the Gemba.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a lean analyst who has mapped many make and repair processes. You are precise about what is waste and what is required, and you show your arithmetic.

Context: Process: [name]. Trigger: [what starts it]. End: [what completes it]. Product family or work type: [description]. Typical batch or order size: [number]. Volume: [per week]. Below is a written description of the steps, from people who do the work. Where known, each step has processing time, waiting time before the next step and walking distance. Times are in [minutes of working time]. Steps required by a customer or an authority (inspections, signatures, records): [list them, or write none].

Process description:
[paste description here]

Task:
1. Step table with columns: Step, Processing time, Waiting time after, Classification, Evidence from the text. Classification is V (the customer would pay for it), N (not value-adding but required, for example by a regulation, a customer or a standard), or W (waste).
2. For every W, name one of the eight wastes: Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilised talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra processing. Quote the words from my description that led you to it.
3. Calculate and show the arithmetic: total processing time, total waiting time, total lead time, and flow efficiency (processing time divided by lead time, as a percentage). Use only numbers I gave. If a time is missing, list it as missing and exclude it, and say how that changes the result.
4. Rank the five wastes with the largest effect on lead time. Label the ranking as Estimate and give the reason.
5. For each of the five, give one or two countermeasure ideas from the lean toolbox (for example 5S, point-of-use storage, SMED, kanban, poka-yoke, standard work, cell layout, pull signals) and one measure that shows whether it worked.
6. List what must be checked at the Gemba before anyone acts, as questions.

Format: Table for step 1, short bullets for the rest. Start with a three-line summary.

Rules: Steps marked as required (N) are not waste, but you may ask whether they are carried out more often or in more places than the requirement says, and flag that as a question, not a recommendation to skip them. Do not invent times, distances or volumes. Mark every assumption with the word Assumption.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented process: a fictional component repair shop, "from goods receipt to ready for NDT". Description (minutes of working time):
1. Goods receipt: 15 min, then waits 480 min for incoming inspection.
2. Incoming inspection: 30 min, waits 960 min for a teardown slot.
3. Teardown: 120 min, the unit is carried 80 m to cleaning, waits 240 min.
4. Cleaning: 45 min, waits 480 min for the NDT booth.
5. NDT: 60 min. Afterwards the paper traveller is retyped into the ERP: 25 min.

Check of the arithmetic Copilot should show:
- Processing time: 15 + 30 + 120 + 45 + 60 + 25 = 295 min.
- Waiting time: 480 + 960 + 240 + 480 = 2,160 min.
- Lead time: 2,455 min. Flow efficiency: 295 / 2,455 = 12.0 percent. Waiting is 88.0 percent of lead time.
- Ranking (Estimate): Waiting for the teardown slot (960 min) is the biggest single item, followed by waiting for incoming inspection and for NDT. Retyping the traveller is Extra processing (25 min) and carrying 80 m is Transportation, both small in time but easy to remove.
- Required steps: incoming inspection and NDT are N, not waste. A good answer asks only whether the 480-minute wait before inspection could be shortened without changing the inspection itself.

WHEN TO USE
When you have a process described in words but no value stream map yet, when a team workshop needs a quick first analysis, or to prepare the Gemba visit for a mapping session. It also works for administrative processes such as order release or engineering change handling.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- A step-by-step description from the people who do the work.
- Processing times and waiting times for as many steps as you can get, in one time unit.
- A list of required steps (regulation, customer, standard) so they are not mislabelled as waste.
- Batch size and volume if you want to discuss inventory.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A step table with classification, the arithmetic for lead time and flow efficiency, a ranked list of five wastes with countermeasure ideas and measures, and a list of questions to verify at the Gemba. The ranking is an estimate for discussion.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Treating required inspections as waste. In regulated fields these are N steps; only question the repetition or the wait around them.
- Using guessed times. A wrong 12 percent flow efficiency can send the team in the wrong direction. Measure two or three real orders first.
- Mixing time units (hours for some steps, minutes for others).
- Taking the Copilot countermeasures as the plan. They are ideas for the team to test.
- Forgetting the waiting time between steps, which is usually where the lead time is.

HOW TO ADAPT
For administrative flows, change the opening to "order release" or "engineering change" and add handoffs as a column. For high-mix repair work, ask for the analysis per work type (for example overhaul versus inspection only). If you have a spreadsheet of step times, attach it instead of pasting the text and ask for the same table. After the analysis, ask a second prompt: "Draft a one-page current-state value stream summary for a workshop with the five largest wastes marked".

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Process descriptions may reveal customer names, programme names or part numbers. Replace them with neutral labels. Cycle times and volumes can be commercially sensitive; check whether your information classification allows them in Copilot. Do not include remarks about named employees. If the process touches regulated records (for example maintenance records), the analysis may suggest efficiency ideas but never decides what is allowed to change; that stays with your quality and compliance functions.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: Lean prompt: draft an A3 problem-solving sheet from messy disruption notes and list the gaps in the evidence
summary: Convert shift logs, emails and chat excerpts about a recurring disruption into a one-page A3 draft with background, current condition, goal, root-cause hypotheses, countermeasures and an evidence-gap list.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are an A3 coach who has taught problem solving on many shop floors. You insist that every statement in the current condition is a fact with a number, and that root causes are separated from guesses.

Context: Problem area: [machine, line, cell or process]. Sponsor role: [role]. Period covered: [from date to date]. Relevant target from our SQDC board or KPI sheet: [target, for example availability 85 percent]. Below are unsorted notes: shift log lines, emails, a few chat messages and my own remarks. Some may contradict each other.

Notes:
[paste notes here]

Task: Draft one A3 with these sections, each with at most five bullets so the sheet fits one page.
1. Background: why this matters, linked to the SQDC target.
2. Current condition: facts only, with numbers, place, time and frequency. Add simple calculations if the numbers allow (for example total lost time, average per event, share by cause) and show them. Mark anything without a number "no number".
3. Goal: a measurable target with a date. I did not give one unless it is stated above, so propose one and mark it Suggested.
4. Root-cause analysis: use 5 Why or the categories Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Environment. Only include causes supported by the notes. Mark every cause that is not yet verified as Hypothesis and say how to verify it.
5. Countermeasures: each linked to one cause, with owner role and a rough effort (S/M/L). Distinguish containment now from permanent fixes.
6. Implementation plan: steps with owner role and week.
7. Follow-up: the measure, the check date and what we standardise if it works.

After the A3 add a gap list: every statement in the sheet that lacks evidence, with the question that would close the gap and the role who can answer it.

Rules: Do not invent numbers, dates or events. Do not name people as causes; describe conditions. If two notes contradict each other, show both and ask which is correct instead of choosing. For anything that could affect product conformity or safety, add the line "Review by quality or safety before action".
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented notes for machine M-12 (fictional), covering four weeks:
- "14 spindle stoppages in 4 weeks, 690 minutes in total."
- "9 of the 14 happened during or right after tool change."
- "Night shift says the new insert grade is the problem, day shift says the tool presetter is off."
- "Target availability for the machine is 85 percent; we are around 78 percent."
- "Maintenance replaced a coolant filter on week 2, no clear effect."

Check of the arithmetic Copilot should show:
- Average stoppage: 690 / 14 = 49.3 minutes.
- Share at or around tool change: 9 / 14 = 64.3 percent of the events.
- Current condition: 14 events, 690 minutes, 64 percent linked to tool change, availability about 78 percent against 85.
- Root cause section lists two competing hypotheses (insert grade, presetter offset), each marked Hypothesis with a check (for example compare presetter readings with a reference tool setter; compare events per insert grade), and does not pick one. The filter replacement is listed as an action with no proven effect.
- Gap list asks: Which minutes of the 690 are tool-change related? Which insert grade was used at each event? Are the 78 percent figures from the same period?

WHEN TO USE
After a repeated or costly disruption, when a team has to move from complaining to a structured analysis, or before a problem-solving workshop to prepare a first draft. Also useful for coaching: let a team lead create the A3 from their own notes and then challenge the gap list together.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The notes, unfiltered, including contradictions.
- The period and the target the problem is measured against.
- Optional: an export of stoppage events as a table, which makes the calculations more reliable.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A one-page A3 draft in seven sections, with calculations shown, hypotheses marked, and a gap list with questions. The team completes and verifies it at the place of work.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Letting Copilot choose between two conflicting stories. Verify with data and write the result in the sheet yourself.
- Skipping the current condition numbers and jumping to countermeasures.
- Accepting a goal that is not measurable. Reword until it names the measure, the value and the date.
- Stopping the 5 Why at a person (for example the operator). Ask why the system allowed it.
- Printing the draft and calling it done. An A3 is a tool for a conversation with the sponsor.

HOW TO ADAPT
For a quality problem, replace the SQDC target with the customer requirement and add a containment line to the background. For a safety event, let the prompt stop at the current condition and containment, and leave the cause analysis to your formal investigation. If your company has an A3 template, paste the section headings and tell Copilot to use them exactly. After the first draft run the 5-Why review prompt from this library to stress-test the cause chain.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Disruption notes often contain names, shift attributions and blame. Strip names and keep roles. Do not paste customer-confidential or export-controlled data unless your rules allow it. If the issue involves an accident or an injury, the formal investigation follows your safety procedure and Copilot is not used as the record. Keep the final signed A3 in your controlled location, not only in the chat.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: Lean prompt: turn SQDC board data and shift notes into a five-minute tier meeting brief
summary: Summarise yesterday's safety, quality, delivery and cost numbers, open actions and shift notes into a short brief with red items, overdue actions, repeat issues and what to escalate to the next tier.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are the assistant of a production area manager who runs a short daily tier meeting at the SQDC board. You are brief, you put safety first, and you never smooth over a red number.

Context: Area: [name]. Date: [date]. Shift covered: [shift]. Targets for today: Safety [target], Quality [target], Delivery [target], Cost [target]. Below are yesterday's actual numbers, the open action list (ID, action, owner role, due date) and short shift notes. Previous days, if I pasted them, are marked as History.

Numbers:
[paste numbers here]

Open actions:
[paste actions here]

Shift notes:
[paste notes here]

History (optional):
[paste previous days or write none]

Task:
1. Status line for each of S, Q, D and C: Green or Red against target, the actual and the target in the same line, and the gap. Show any calculation (for example scrap percentage = scrapped parts divided by produced parts).
2. The three topics for the meeting. Order: safety first, then the largest gap to target. For each, one sentence of fact and one open question for the owner.
3. Open actions: those overdue (with the number of days overdue), those due today and those due this week.
4. Repeating issues: anything that also appears in the History or in more than one shift note.
5. Escalate to the next tier: what the team cannot solve at this level, with the specific ask and a suggested date.
6. Two questions the meeting leader should ask the team.

Format: Maximum 300 words plus the action table. A person must be able to read it aloud in about five minutes. No introduction, no closing remarks.

Rules: Use only the data I provided. If a number is missing, say "no data" instead of estimating. Do not name individuals; use roles. Do not mark anything Green if the data is missing.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented data for "Cell 4", one day:
- Safety: 0 incidents, 1 near miss (pallet near walkway). Target 0 incidents.
- Quality: 220 parts produced, 4 scrapped. Target scrap at most 1.0 percent.
- Delivery: 20 orders due, 18 shipped on time. Target 95 percent on time.
- Cost: overtime 12 h against a budget of 8 h.
- Actions: A-31 "Mark walkway", due 3 days ago; A-35 "Order spare insert holders", due today.
- Shift note: "Late shift waited 40 minutes for a crane."

Check of the arithmetic Copilot should show:
- Scrap: 4 / 220 = 1.8 percent against 1.0 percent: Red.
- Delivery: 18 / 20 = 90 percent against 95 percent: Red (two orders late).
- Cost: 12 h against 8 h budget = 4 h over: Red.
- Safety: no incident is Green on the target, but the near miss is the first topic because safety comes first.
- A-31 is 3 days overdue and linked to the near miss; this is the first escalation question. The crane wait goes to the next tier if it repeats.

WHEN TO USE
Every day before the tier 1 or tier 2 meeting, when the board is filled by hand and shift notes are spread over several channels. It also works as a Monday summary of the whole previous week if you paste the daily numbers.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- Daily SQDC numbers with targets (pasted from the board, an Excel table or a Power BI export).
- The open action list with owner roles and due dates.
- Short shift notes (a few lines per shift).
- Optional: the last three to five days for pattern detection.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Four status lines, three meeting topics, overdue actions, repeating issues, escalation asks and two questions, in under 300 words. It is a brief for the leader, not the minutes.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Letting the summary hide a Red behind a good story. Keep the actual and target in every line.
- Pasting numbers without targets, so Copilot has to guess what Green means.
- Making the brief longer than the meeting. The limit of 300 words is the point.
- Treating Copilot's repeat-issue detection as complete. It only sees what you pasted.
- Skipping the escalation block, which is the main reason for a tier structure.

HOW TO ADAPT
Replace S, Q, D and C with the categories your board uses (for example add Environment or People). Change the thresholds for Red and Amber in the context if you use three colours. If the numbers sit in an Excel file, attach the file and ask Copilot to read the sheet named [sheet]. For tier 2 or 3, paste the escalations from several tier 1 briefs and ask for one combined list sorted by safety and customer impact. If you use Teams, you can have the meeting notes recorded and reuse them as the shift notes of the next day, if recording is permitted in your organisation.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Daily numbers about output, scrap and delivery may be commercially sensitive; check your information classification. Shift notes can contain names and complaints about individuals; use roles and keep personnel topics out. Do not use the brief for individual performance evaluation, which usually needs works council involvement. Safety incidents are recorded in your safety system, not in a chat.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. title: Lean prompt: stress-test a 5-Why chain for logic jumps, blame, missing evidence and the escape cause
summary: Paste a written 5-Why analysis and let Copilot check each link, separate fact from opinion, spot blame and symptom-level causes, and list the checks needed before the root cause is accepted.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a sceptical problem-solving reviewer in a regulated manufacturing company. You are fair but you do not accept a root cause just because it sounds plausible. You review the reasoning, not the people.

Context: Problem statement as written by the team: [paste problem statement]. The 5-Why chain as written: [paste chain, one why per line]. Evidence the team says it has: [records, measurements, photos, interviews, or none]. Scope: [process, product, period]. The team has authority to change: [what the team can control, for example work instructions, tooling, planning rules; not for example supplier contracts].

Task:
1. Review the problem statement. It should be specific, measurable, and contain neither a cause nor a solution. Say what is missing.
2. For every link, read it backwards with "Because X, therefore Y" and rate it: Sound, Weak or Jump, with a one-line reason.
3. For every why, classify the evidence: Fact (a record or measurement exists), Opinion, or Hypothesis (plausible but unchecked). Do not assume that evidence exists unless I listed it.
4. Detect these patterns and quote the line: a person or "human error" as the stopping point; blame words; a cause at symptom level; a single chain where several parallel causes are plausible (propose branches as questions); a final cause the team cannot control.
5. Test the end of the chain: if this cause were removed, would the original problem have been prevented? Also check whether the chain explains why the problem was not detected earlier (the escape cause) and say if that is missing.
6. For each Weak or Jump link, give the one question or check that would produce evidence (for example "compare tool-life records for the last 10 lots"). Do not invent the answer.
7. Verdict: Accept, Accept with checks, or Rework, with a three-line reason.

Format: Table with columns Link, Text, Rating, Evidence status, Comment. Then the numbered findings.

Rules: Do not rewrite the root cause for the team. Do not invent evidence. If you suggest a branch, phrase it as a question to investigate. Keep the tone neutral and constructive.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented problem: "Burrs found on 6 of 40 brackets at final inspection on 12 March, line 2." Chain:
1. Why? The operator did not deburr those parts.
2. Why? The operator was in a hurry.
3. Why? The planner overloaded the shift.
4. Why? There are not enough people.
5. Why? Management does not care about quality.
Evidence listed: none.

What a good review contains:
- Problem statement: reasonably specific (6 of 40 is 15 percent), but it does not say which operation or when the burr appears.
- Link 1 is a Jump and an Opinion ("did not deburr" is not checked; maybe the deburr step was not in the routing). Links 2 to 4 are Hypotheses. Link 5 is blame and an Opinion, and is not controllable by the team.
- Pattern found: stops at a person, blame wording, single chain only. Branch questions: Is deburring in the work instruction and routing? Is the deburr tool available? Was the burr created by a worn cutter at the previous operation?
- Escape cause missing: why did the in-process check not find it?
- Verdict: Rework, with checks listed (routing, tool-life records, in-process inspection plan).

WHEN TO USE
Before a root cause goes into an A3, an 8D, a corrective action request or a management review. Also as a coaching tool: run it on a draft from a team lead and discuss the findings together. It is most valuable where an auditor or customer will challenge your cause analysis.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The problem statement and the written chain.
- A list of the evidence the team really has (records, measurements, photos).
- The scope and the span of control of the team.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A table that rates every link, a list of detected patterns, the escape-cause check, specific checks to get evidence and a verdict. It improves the reasoning; the team still has to collect the facts.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Handing over only the answers without the evidence list. The review then cannot tell fact from opinion.
- Letting Copilot propose a root cause and presenting it as the finding. Ask for questions, not answers.
- Ignoring the escape cause. A cause chain that explains only occurrence invites the same problem later.
- Treating Accept as proof. Only verification in the process proves a root cause.
- Using it to judge people. Review the chain, not who wrote it.

HOW TO ADAPT
For fishbone-based analyses, paste the categories and causes instead of a chain and ask for the same ratings. For an 8D, run it on D4 only. For a safety investigation follow your formal method and use this only as a second reader. Add a rule such as "Treat training as a root cause only if the training record shows a gap" to match your culture. Combine it with the A3 prompt from this library: draft first, review second.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Root-cause chains can contain names, job titles and customer or part identifiers. Anonymise before pasting. In aviation or other regulated settings, the cause analysis recorded in your quality system is the official one; this review is a thinking aid. Do not paste the content of confidential audits or customer data unless your rules allow it.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: MRO prompt: turn raw shift notes into a structured handover per aircraft for review by the outgoing certifying staff
summary: Structure rough shift notes into a per-registration handover with completed, open and new items, parts status and VERIFY flags. A draft for the outgoing team to check, never a release or a record.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You structure shift handover notes for an aircraft maintenance organisation. You do not decide airworthiness, you do not write release statements, you do not fill gaps, and you do not rewrite technical findings. You only organise what is in the notes.

Context: Station: [station]. Handover from [early / late / night] shift to [next shift], date [date]. Aircraft by registration: [list]. Our handover headings, taken from our procedure: [paste the headings required by your handover procedure; if none, use: Work completed, Work in progress and exact stage, Deferred or open items, New defects found, Defects closed, Parts and material status, Special tools and equipment, Items awaiting inspection or independent inspection, General issues]. Raw notes from the outgoing shift:
[paste notes here]

Task:
1. Group the notes by registration, then by work order or task card reference. Notes that name no aircraft go under "General".
2. Under each heading write what the notes say, quoting technical wording as written. If the notes say nothing for a heading, write: "Nothing reported in notes, outgoing shift to confirm". Never write just "none".
3. Add the flag VERIFY to every item where the notes are ambiguous: no task card or defect card number, unclear stage of work, unclear who is meant, parts without part number or serial number, an item described as done without any mention of sign-off or inspection.
4. Items for the first hour of the next shift: aircraft with an upcoming departure or inspection, parts or tools expected, work that was stopped mid-task.
5. Contradictions: list notes that disagree with each other.
6. Questions for the outgoing staff: at most eight, most important first.

Format: A header block per aircraft (Registration, Work package, Outgoing role, Incoming role), then a table with the headings as rows. At the very top write: "DRAFT structured from raw notes. Not a record. Must be reviewed and confirmed by the outgoing certifying staff or shift lead according to our MOE."

Rules: Use only wording from the notes. Do not add task references, torque values, limits, intervals or manual references that are not in the notes. Never state that anything is serviceable, complete, airworthy or released. Say "reported as completed in notes, sign-off status per task card to be checked" instead of "completed".
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented notes (fictional registrations ZZ-ABC and ZZ-DEF, no real aircraft):
"ZZ-ABC A-check cards 12 to 31 done except 27, waiting for access panel seals, on order, ETA Thursday. Found corrosion on cargo floor beam, raised defect card DC-0417, NDT not looked at yet. ZZ-DEF left main gear wheel change ongoing, new wheel fitted, torque not done yet. Borescope battery dead. Heard ZZ-DEF departure moved to 06:00?"

What a good answer contains:
- ZZ-ABC: cards 12 to 31 except 27 reported as completed in notes, sign-off to be checked (VERIFY). Card 27 open, waiting for seals on order, ETA Thursday (VERIFY: part number missing). New defect DC-0417, corrosion on cargo floor beam, NDT not started. Items awaiting inspection: NDT for DC-0417.
- ZZ-DEF: wheel change in progress, new wheel fitted, torque not done yet (VERIFY: no task card number, part and serial numbers missing). First hour of next shift: confirm departure time because the note carries a question mark.
- General: borescope battery dead, tooling to confirm.
- Headings with no information show "Nothing reported in notes, outgoing shift to confirm".
- Questions include: What are the task card numbers for ZZ-DEF? Was card 12 to 31 sign-off done for all? Who raised the corrosion defect and what is the location detail?

WHEN TO USE
At the end of a shift in a Part-145 or similar organisation when the outgoing team has rough notes (a whiteboard, a messaging thread, a notebook) and wants a complete, consistent handover, or when the incoming shift lead wants a quick check that nothing was missed. The handover itself must follow the procedure in your own exposition; this prompt only helps you prepare the content.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The raw notes from the outgoing shift.
- The handover headings from your procedure (copy them from the MOE section on shift handover).
- The list of aircraft registrations and work packages in work.
- Optionally, the open defect card list as a table so the notes can be matched.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A draft handover per registration with the required headings, VERIFY flags, first-hour items, contradictions and questions, with a warning line at the top. The outgoing certifying staff or shift lead checks, corrects and completes it before it is used as the handover in your system.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Using the Copilot text as the handover record. The record is what your procedure and system say it is, completed by the people responsible.
- Letting empty headings be silently dropped. A heading that says nothing was reported is itself information; the prompt keeps it visible.
- Pasting notes that name task cards by memory. Add the real numbers from the work package first.
- Allowing Copilot to rephrase technical findings. Keep the original wording to avoid meaning drift.
- Skipping the oral handover. Written notes support the conversation, they do not replace it.

HOW TO ADAPT
Replace the default headings with those in your handover procedure. Add a column Station for multi-hangar operations. For component or workshop shifts, group by work order instead of registration. Ask for a shorter version (maximum ten lines per aircraft) for the shift briefing slide. To reduce effort, ask the outgoing staff to dictate notes at the aircraft and paste the transcript. If your organisation uses a digital handover tool, treat this prompt as a way to check completeness before entering the data there.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Release and certification stay with certifying staff and the persons named in your MOE. A Copilot output is never a release, never a task card sign-off and never a substitute for the manual or the work card. Handover requirements come from the applicable regulation and your approved procedures; check against the current regulation (for aviation maintenance, the Part-145 requirement on information transfer at shift change, a point commonly cited as 145.A.47(c), though you should confirm the wording) and your MOE before relying on any summary. Remove names of staff and any customer-confidential data unless your rules allow them. If your organisation processes personal data of staff in handover notes, consult your data protection officer and the works council before introducing AI support.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: Procurement prompt: write a firm but fair late-delivery chaser with facts, impact and a dated commitment request
summary: Draft three escalation levels of a supplier chaser email from PO facts and impact: standard reminder, escalation with impact and a last step before formal escalation, each asking for a confirmed date.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a strategic buyer in a manufacturing company that supplies regulated industries. You write short, factual emails in clear business English. You are firm and fair, you never threaten, and you always ask for a dated commitment.

Context: Purchase order [PO number], line [line], part [part number and description], quantity ordered [number], quantity received so far [number], original delivery date [date], current supplier promise [date or none], today is [date]. Previous chasers: [number, with dates]. Impact on us: [for example line stoppage on date, customer delivery on date, or none yet]. Relationship: [strategic / regular / spot supplier]. Supplier contact role: [for example sales manager or planner]. Contract terms: [paste the clause text if you want it mentioned; otherwise write do not mention terms]. Facts, status notes and anything the supplier already told us:
[paste notes here]

Task: Write three versions of the email.
A. Standard reminder: polite, short, asks for confirmation of the delivery date.
B. Escalation with impact: adds the effect on our schedule and asks for a recovery plan.
C. Last step before formal escalation: factual, states what happens next inside our company in neutral wording, sets a response deadline.

Every version has:
- Subject line with PO number and part number.
- First sentence: the ask.
- A small fact table: PO and line, part, quantity ordered, quantity received, original date, current promise, days late (calculate from my dates and show it).
- Specific asks: (1) a confirmed delivery date by [response deadline], (2) whether a partial shipment is possible, (3) the cause in one line and the recovery plan, (4) a named contact for follow-up.
- A closing line with the next step after the deadline.

Format: Three emails, each under 170 words plus the table. After them, list any fact you needed but did not have, written as [missing: description].

Rules: No threats, no sarcasm, no blame words. Do not cite contract clauses, penalties or legal consequences unless I pasted the clause. Do not invent dates, quantities or promises. Keep the same facts in all three versions.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented facts: PO 45001234, line 20, part BRK-2210-A "bracket assembly", ordered 400, received 0, original delivery 10 Nov, supplier promise 17 Nov, today 20 Nov, one earlier chaser on 12 Nov. Impact: our assembly line 4 runs out of brackets on 27 Nov. Strategic supplier. Response deadline: 22 Nov, 12:00.

Check of the arithmetic Copilot should show:
- Days late against the original date: 10 Nov to 20 Nov = 10 days. Days past the supplier promise: 17 Nov to 20 Nov = 3 days.
- Runway on our side: 20 Nov to 27 Nov = 7 days. Version B mentions this date, not a vague "urgent".
- Version A asks for a confirmed date and thanks the supplier for the earlier answer. Version B asks for a recovery plan, partial shipment of at least what line 4 needs by 27 Nov, and names the impact. Version C states that if no date is confirmed by 22 Nov, 12:00, the issue goes to the procurement lead and to quality for a joint call, with no threats.
- Footer: [missing: supplier's stated reason for the delay], [missing: contact name].

WHEN TO USE
When a delivery is late and you must choose the tone before a deadline, when you have to chase many open lines and want consistent wording, or when you want to give a new buyer a model for each escalation level. If your ERP flags late lines, paste the facts for one line at a time.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- PO number, line, part, quantities, original and promised dates.
- Number and dates of earlier reminders.
- A concrete impact with a date, or an explicit statement that there is none.
- Response deadline and the contact role.
- Contract text only if you want it mentioned.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Three ready-to-edit emails (reminder, escalation, last step) with identical facts, a fact table, specific asks and a list of missing facts. You choose, adjust and send. Nothing is sent automatically.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Sending version C first. Start at the level that fits the history and the impact.
- Vague deadlines such as ASAP. A date and time make the commitment checkable.
- Mentioning penalties from memory. Only quote a clause you have checked with your contracts team.
- Forgetting the quality angle for regulated parts: a rushed partial shipment still needs full documentation. Ask for the paperwork with the parts.
- Writing in anger. If the email feels emotional, ask Copilot to remove emotional wording and keep the facts.

HOW TO ADAPT
Switch the language of the email in the context line (for example German or French) and the tone for your culture. For direct materials with long lead times, add a line asking for the lead time of the replacement order. For call-off orders, replace the PO fact table with the schedule line. For a supplier scorecard, add the task: "Add one sentence I can paste into the supplier scorecard comments". If you use Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, check the current documentation for the Supplier Communications Agent, which can draft reminders for orders; its availability and cost can change, and the buyer still reviews each draft. This prompt works without it.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Supplier contact details and prices are confidential business data. Paste only what is needed. Do not paste complete contracts or drawings; paste the one clause if required. Part numbers for export-controlled items can be restricted; check with your export control officer. Never send a Copilot draft without reading it; you are accountable for what leaves your company. For regulated products, delays can affect certificates and traceability documents, so quality has to be informed through your normal process.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: Quality prompt: rewrite a work instruction into short unambiguous steps without changing its technical meaning
summary: Turn a long or vague work instruction into numbered one-action steps, with a table of preserved values, flagged ambiguities and a change summary the document owner can check line by line.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a technical writer for manufacturing work instructions. You write in plain, direct language that non-native speakers can follow. You change wording, never technical meaning, and you never fill in missing values.

Context: Document: [title, ID, revision]. Audience: [for example operators with six months of experience, some with English as a second language]. This is a controlled document: your rewrite is a proposal for the document owner, not a new revision. Standards for the rewrite: one action per step, imperative verb first, sentences of at most [20] words, warnings placed before the step they apply to. Source text:
[paste source text here]

Task:
1. Rewrite the instruction as numbered steps.
2. Preserved values table: list every number, unit, tolerance, part number, tool, material, reference and time exactly as in the source, with the source sentence beside it, so the owner can verify nothing changed.
3. Warnings and cautions: keep those in the source, placed in front of the step they belong to. Use WARNING for risk of injury and CAUTION for risk of damage to product or equipment. Do not add new ones. Under "Suggested safety review" list candidates the owner might consider, as questions.
4. Ambiguities: list vague terms, unclear pronouns, undefined sequences, missing acceptance criteria, missing tools, conditions such as "if necessary" without a trigger. For each, give the question the owner must answer. In the steps, mark each gap as [value from document owner].
5. Change summary table: Source sentence, New step, Meaning changed? (No, or Possible with an explanation).
6. Where would a photo, sketch or checklist remove text? List up to five places.

Format: Steps first, then the four tables and lists. No commentary before the steps.

Rules: Do not invent values, tolerances, times, tools or warnings. Do not merge steps that contain different inspection points, hold points or sign-offs. Keep hold points and sign-offs exactly where the source has them. Do not translate technical terms or standard names. If a sentence can be read in two ways, keep both readings in the ambiguity list and do not choose.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented source sentence (not a real instruction): "Clean the surface properly and apply the sealant, not too thick, then wait until it is slightly tacky, and check it. If necessary repeat."

What a good answer contains:
- Steps: "1. Clean the surface with [cleaning agent from document owner]. 2. Apply sealant to a thickness of [value from document owner]. 3. Wait until the sealant reaches [tack condition or time from document owner]. 4. Check the sealant against [acceptance criterion from document owner]. 5. Repeat steps 1 to 4 if [trigger from document owner]."
- Ambiguities: "properly" (no cleaning agent, no cleanliness criterion), "not too thick" (no value), "slightly tacky" (no condition or time), "check it" (no method or acceptance criterion), "if necessary repeat" (no trigger, no maximum number of repeats), "it" (the surface or the sealant).
- Preserved values: none in the source, and the answer says so, which is itself a finding.
- Suggested safety review (questions only): ventilation or protective equipment for cleaning agent and sealant, to be decided by the owner.
- Change summary: step 5 meaning changed? Possible: the original repeats "it", which could mean only the check or the whole sequence.

WHEN TO USE
When an instruction is long, ambiguous or written for experts and a new or international team has to follow it, before a document revision, or when an audit or incident found that people interpret a step differently. Also good for creating a plain-language draft for training. In regulated fields the controlled revision still goes through your normal approval path.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The source text, including notes and warnings, as text (not a screenshot).
- The document ID and revision, for traceability of your proposal.
- The audience and the language level.
- The sentence length and warning conventions you use.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A rewritten step list, a table of preserved values, flagged warnings, a list of ambiguities with questions to the owner, a change summary and a list of places where a picture would help. The owner decides what goes into the next revision.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Replacing the controlled document with the rewrite. It is a proposal that follows the change process.
- Not checking the preserved values table against the source. This is the control that catches silent changes.
- Letting Copilot fill in missing values to make the text feel complete. The placeholders are the honest result.
- Merging steps and losing a hold point or sign-off.
- Skipping the shop-floor test. Have an operator follow the new steps once and watch where they hesitate.

HOW TO ADAPT
For a company style guide, paste its rules into the context. If you use Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100) or a similar controlled language, name it and paste the rules or approved word list you have; do not assume Copilot recalls the dictionary exactly. For a quick reference card, ask for a version with at most eight steps and the three critical points highlighted. For a multi-language shopfloor, ask for the plain-English version first, review it, and only then have it translated and reviewed by a competent speaker. For visuals, ask for a photo shot list with what each picture must show.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Work instructions may contain proprietary processes, customer requirements or export-controlled technical data. Check your classification and your customer agreements before pasting. For safety or product-critical steps (torque, cure, inspection, special processes) the technical authority reviews every change, and an aircraft or product release never depends on a Copilot rewrite. Keep the approved revision in your document control system as the only valid version.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. title: Quality prompt: brainstorm FMEA failure modes, effects and causes for a process step as a draft for the team
summary: Generate a structured list of failure modes, effects, causes and controls for one process step, with draft ratings and RPN calculation using your own scales, for the cross-functional team to correct.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a process FMEA facilitator. You help a cross-functional team to think broadly before the workshop, and you are explicit that all ratings are drafts for the team to decide.

Context: Process step: [step name and short description]. Function or requirement of the step: [what the step must achieve]. Product and characteristic: [part, feature, tolerance or requirement]. Equipment and tooling: [list]. Existing prevention controls: [list, or none known]. Existing detection controls: [list, or none known]. Known history (scrap, complaints, past findings): [list, or none]. Our rating scales for Severity, Occurrence and Detection (1 to 10) are the table below. Use them exactly.

Rating scales:
[paste your Severity, Occurrence and Detection scale tables here]

Task:
1. List up to [10] potential failure modes for this step. A failure mode is how the step could fail to meet its function. For each give: failure mode, effects (on the next step and on the end customer), potential causes, current prevention controls and current detection controls. Take controls only from my input; if I gave none, write "none known".
2. Suggest preliminary ratings for Severity, Occurrence and Detection. For each rating, name the row of my scale it comes from. Mark every rating Draft, team decides. Calculate RPN = Severity x Occurrence x Detection and show the multiplication.
3. Flag every failure mode with Severity of [9] or higher, regardless of RPN, because a low RPN can hide a severe effect.
4. Sort the table by RPN, then give a second list sorted by Severity.
5. For the top five, suggest recommended actions. Name preventive actions first (for example poka-yoke, fixture design, standard work, tool-life management), detection actions second.
6. Possible gaps: scan the categories material, method, machine, measurement, environment and human interface and name failure modes that may be missing.
7. List the data the team needs to rate Occurrence and Detection properly, for example scrap history or capability data.

Format: One table for steps 1 and 2, then the lists. Start with a one-line reminder that the ratings are conversation starters.

Rules: Do not invent history, defect rates or capability values. If you lack data for Occurrence, say so and give a range with the reason instead of one number. If a failure mode may affect safety or a safety-critical characteristic, write "Severity to be decided by design authority or engineering".
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented step: "Drill and countersink holes in a bracket" (a fictional part). Controls given: prevention, tool-life counter; detection, 100 percent go/no-go gauge by the operator. Illustrative scales only, not your company's scale.

Example rows Copilot might return (Draft, team decides):
- Hole diameter oversize. Effect: part scrapped, possible rework. Cause: worn drill. Ratings S 7, O 4, D 3. RPN = 7 x 4 x 3 = 84.
- Countersink too deep. Effect: reduced fastener seating, possible reject at final check. Cause: depth stop set wrongly after tool change. S 8, O 3, D 5. RPN = 8 x 3 x 5 = 120.
- Burr left at hole exit. Effect: assembly interference, damage to the mating part. Cause: dull drill or missing deburr step. S 5, O 6, D 4. RPN = 5 x 6 x 4 = 120.

The sorted list shows two rows with the same RPN of 120, so the severity list helps decide which to discuss first (countersink too deep, S 8). The data list asks for scrap by cause and the detection method for the countersink depth, since the go/no-go gauge only checks diameter.

WHEN TO USE
To prepare an FMEA workshop, to open up a thin FMEA with new ideas, when you introduce a new process step or a changed supplier, or to reuse a previous FMEA as a starting point. The value is breadth: it can name failure modes the team forgets. It does not replace the team's experience with the real process.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- Step description, function, characteristic, equipment.
- Existing prevention and detection controls.
- History data if you have it.
- Your own Severity, Occurrence and Detection scale tables.
- The Severity level you always want flagged.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A table of failure modes with effects, causes, controls, draft ratings and RPN, two sorted lists, flagged severe items, recommended actions for the top five, possible gaps and a list of data to gather.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Using Copilot's ratings as the result. The team rates, from data and experience.
- Not pasting your scale. Then the ratings float without a basis.
- Ranking only by RPN. A severe effect with a low RPN still needs attention.
- Listing detection as the main action. Prefer prevention in the process.
- Accepting invented controls. The prompt asks for controls only from your input.

HOW TO ADAPT
If your FMEA procedure follows the AIAG and VDA FMEA handbook, which uses Action Priority instead of RPN, replace step 2 with "Propose preliminary ratings and look up Action Priority only from the table I pasted" and paste the table; do not let Copilot recall the table from memory. For a design FMEA, change the context to function, interfaces and design characteristics. For a service or MRO task, describe the task and the error modes of omitted steps, wrong parts or damage while working. Keep the output as a first column set for your Excel FMEA sheet.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
FMEA content describes product weaknesses and is usually confidential. Anonymise customer and part names where possible and respect your customer and export-control agreements. The Severity of safety-related or flight-critical effects is decided by the responsible engineering and safety authority, not by Copilot. The signed FMEA remains in your quality system, and the AI draft is only an input.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. Microsoft Learn documents that prompts and responses in Copilot Chat with a work account fall under the Data Protection Addendum and are not used to train foundation models. title: Quality prompt: draft an 8D report from the facts you have and flag every section the evidence does not yet support
summary: Build a D0 to D8 draft from complaint facts, with an is/is-not problem description, containment scope, occurrence and escape causes and an evidence status per section plus a customer-readiness check.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a quality engineer with long experience in 8D reports for customer complaints and supplier corrective action requests. You write factually and you refuse to present guesses as findings.

Context: We are the [supplier / customer]. Complaint reference: [reference]. Product: [part number and description]. Quantity affected: [number]. Detected on [date] at [place or process step] by [role]. Customer requirements for the 8D: [format, due dates, for example containment within 24 hours, full report in 30 days, or none known]. Facts, records and notes collected so far (measurements, inspection records, process data, photos described in words, emails):
[paste facts here]

Task: Draft the 8D with these sections.
D0 Symptom and need for emergency response.
D1 Team: roles only.
D2 Problem description using Is and Is not: what, where, when, how many, and how detected. Quantify with a calculation where numbers allow, and show it.
D3 Interim containment: actions, scope (stock, work in progress, in transit, at the customer), verification of the containment, date, owner role.
D4 Root cause: separate the occurrence cause (why it happened) from the escape cause (why it was not detected). State the evidence for each.
D5 Permanent corrective actions: chosen actions, planned verification.
D6 Implementation and validation: planned dates, how effectiveness will be shown.
D7 Prevent recurrence: systemic measures (FMEA, control plan, procedures, training, similar products or lines).
D8 Closure and recognition of the team.

For every section add a status: Evidenced, Partly evidenced, or Open. For Partly and Open sections, list what evidence is needed and which role provides it.

After D8 add a customer-readiness check: the questions a critical customer reviewer would ask about this draft.

Rules: Do not say containment is complete unless my facts say so. Do not call a root cause confirmed unless my facts show verification. "Human error" or "operator mistake" is not accepted as a root cause: ask why the system allowed it. Use only dates from my facts. Do not blame people or suppliers by name. Keep each section short; use bullets.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented facts: "A customer found 12 of 300 delivered housings with bore diameter out of tolerance at incoming inspection. Our final inspection takes 5 pieces per lot. Tool change records show the cutting insert was replaced on the day the lot was machined, no first-piece measurement recorded afterwards. Other lots from the same week not yet checked."

What a good answer contains:
- D2: 12 / 300 = 4.0 percent of the delivered lot; our sample of 5 pieces; Is not: other lots, unknown, not yet checked.
- D3: Open. Needs scope (stock, WIP, other lots of the same week, parts in transit) and a sorting or 100 percent check plan with owner and date.
- D4: Occurrence is a hypothesis: insert changed without first-piece check (Partly evidenced, needs measurement data and tool-life records). Escape: sampling 5 pieces from 300 gives limited chance to find a 4 percent defect; the Copilot draft should only state that it is a weak detection method and ask for the sampling plan basis, not invent probabilities.
- D5 to D7: Open, with suggested directions as questions (first-piece check after tool change; in-process gauge) marked Suggested.
- Customer-readiness check: What was the containment at the customer? Which other lots are affected? How do you know the insert change caused it?

WHEN TO USE
When a complaint or supplier corrective action request arrives with a short deadline and you have scattered facts, to create a first D0 to D3 within the containment window, or to prepare the full report. It helps with structure and consistency. The investigation work itself still happens with data and the team.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- Complaint details and customer format requirements.
- Facts, records and measurements gathered, with dates.
- The people or roles in the team.
- Any existing process documents (control plan, inspection plan) described in text.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A D0 to D8 draft with an evidence status per section, a list of missing evidence by role, and a customer-readiness check. Use it as the working document of the team, replace each Open section with real findings and have the quality lead approve before sending.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Filling every section to look complete. Open sections are honest and tell the team what to do next.
- Sending a draft containment as if it were done. The customer reads containment as a commitment.
- Writing 'retrain the operator' as the corrective action without a systemic cause.
- Ignoring the escape cause. Customers often check it first.
- Not confirming dates. Copilot uses only your dates, so check the timeline once more yourself.

HOW TO ADAPT
Match the section titles to the customer's template (some use different names for D4 to D7) and paste the template headings. For internal problems, replace "customer" with "next process step" and keep the same logic. For a supplier 8D that you receive, switch the task to "Review the supplier's 8D against the criteria above and list weaknesses". Combine it with the 5-Why review prompt in this library for D4 and with the nonconformance review prompt for the initial description. In aviation, add "check whether the issue triggers a reporting or notification obligation under our procedures" as a question list for quality, not as an answer.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Complaint data includes customer names, part numbers and often confidential drawings. Anonymise where your agreement requires it. Do not paste personal data of staff or customer employees. Customer and regulatory notification obligations, and any statement about product conformity or airworthiness, belong to your quality and certification functions. The 8D that goes to the customer is the signed document from your quality system, not the chat output.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. title: Quality prompt: review a nonconformance report for completeness, objective wording and traceability before submission
summary: Check an NCR text against your template fields, spot opinion and blame wording, missing requirement references and inconsistent counts, and get a neutral rewrite of the description with missing items marked.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a peer reviewer in quality assurance for a regulated manufacturing or maintenance company. You check that a nonconformance report is complete, factual and traceable. You do not decide disposition, and you do not add facts.

Context: Our NCR template has these fields: [list the fields, for example NCR number, part number, serial or batch, order number, quantity, location, detection point, detected by (role), requirement violated with document and revision, description, containment, attachments]. Our rules: the description states facts only (what, where, how many, how detected, versus which requirement); disposition (use as is, rework, repair, scrap, return to supplier) is decided by [MRB / authorised engineering and quality], never by the writer; classification of severity is done by [role]. NCR text to review:
[paste the NCR text and field values here]

Task:
1. Completeness table: field, Present / Missing / Unclear, comment.
2. Objectivity: quote every phrase that is opinion, blame, speculation, emotion or vague ("again", "obviously", "as usual", "sloppy"), and propose a neutral replacement that keeps all facts.
3. Requirement: is the violated requirement stated with document, revision and clause or characteristic? If not, ask for it. Do not guess clause numbers or limits.
4. Quantification: check counts, measured values against tolerance, and units. Flag inconsistencies (for example a different number of parts in the title and in the text). Show any arithmetic.
5. Traceability: do part number, serial or batch, order and location agree across the text? List mismatches.
6. Mixing of content: mark parts of the text that are really root cause, corrective action or disposition request, and say where they belong.
7. Escalation questions: list questions the quality lead should answer, for example whether the finding could be a suspected unapproved part, could affect product safety or airworthiness, could affect other lots, or needs customer notification. Do not answer them.
8. Rewrite only the description field, using only facts from the text, with [missing: description] marks where information is absent.

Format: Table for step 1, bullets for the rest, rewritten description at the end.

Rules: Do not add facts, measurements or part numbers. Do not propose a disposition. Keep technical wording as written.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented NCR text: "Idiot operator drilled the hole wrong again. The brackets from last week are scrap, about 5 or 6 pieces. Please approve rework."

What a good answer contains:
- Completeness: part number, serial or batch, order, requirement, detection point and measured value all Missing; quantity Unclear.
- Objectivity: "Idiot operator" is blame and insult; "again" refers to an unreferenced earlier event; "wrong" is vague. Neutral replacement: "A hole in [part number] was found [position and nature of deviation: missing]."
- Quantification: "5 or 6 pieces" is inconsistent; the NCR needs one counted number and the identification of each piece.
- Mixing: "scrap" and "approve rework" are disposition statements and contradict each other, so they belong to the disposition step, decided by the authorised role.
- Escalation questions: Which requirement was violated? Are other brackets from the same lot affected? Is there a measured value?
- Rewritten description: "Deviation found on [number of pieces: missing] [part number: missing], [batch or serial: missing], on [date: missing], at [detection point: missing]. [Measured value and requirement: missing]."

WHEN TO USE
Before an NCR is submitted or sent to a supplier or customer, during quality coaching of new writers, or during a backlog clean-up when many NCRs have inconsistent texts. It is also a good teaching tool: show the review to production staff to learn what a good description looks like.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The NCR text and all field values.
- Your template fields and rules for description and disposition.
- Optionally, the controlling document and revision numbers so the review can compare them.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A completeness table, quoted wording problems with neutral replacements, a requirement and quantity check, traceability mismatches, a list of misplaced content, escalation questions and a rewritten description with missing items marked.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Letting Copilot suggest the disposition. That belongs to the authorised role.
- Fixing wording but not the missing facts. A polished NCR with missing evidence is still weak.
- Skipping the escalation questions for suspected unapproved parts or airworthiness effects. Your procedure defines who decides.
- Mixing the root cause into the description. Keep description, cause and action separate.
- Pasting NCRs with customer data without checking your agreements.

HOW TO ADAPT
Replace the template fields with yours. For supplier NCRs, add the supplier's requirements and ask to check the text for use as a supplier corrective action request. For maintenance, change the fields to aircraft registration, task card, defect card and component data, and add "check that the finding is separated from any statement of airworthiness". For training, ask for a score per field and a list of the three most common weaknesses over several NCRs you paste (anonymised). Run the 8D prompt next if the NCR triggers a corrective action.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
NCRs include part numbers, supplier and customer names and sometimes personal names. Anonymise as required by your agreements and do not paste restricted or export-controlled technical data unless allowed. Review of suspected unapproved parts, notifications to customers or authorities and any decision on conformity or airworthiness follow your procedures and are never delegated to Copilot. The valid NCR is the one in your quality system.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. Microsoft Learn documents that prompts and responses in Copilot Chat with a work account fall under the Data Protection Addendum and are not used to train foundation models. Web search queries are handled separately (sent to Bing, outside that commitment), so ask your admin how web search is configured and keep confidential details out of prompts when it is on.

title: Audit prompt: build a risk-based internal audit question list for a process from your procedure and past findings
summary: Turn a process procedure, last audit findings and KPIs into ranked audit risk areas, open questions with evidence to request, trace samples, role interviews and a timed plan for a 90-minute audit.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are an experienced internal auditor for management systems in a manufacturing or maintenance organisation. You audit by sampling evidence and tracing real examples, not by reading the procedure aloud. You do not decide findings; the auditor decides on evidence.

Context: Process audited: [process name]. Management system standard in scope: [for example ISO 9001, AS9100, AS9110, ISO 14001; I will paste requirement text if I want clauses referenced]. Audit duration: [90] minutes. Auditee roles: [process owner, supervisor, operator, others]. Below: the procedure text, the findings of the last audit of this process, current KPIs and recent changes (people, tools, systems, products), recent incidents or complaints.

Procedure:
[paste procedure text here]

Last audit findings and open corrective actions:
[paste findings here or write none]

KPIs, changes, incidents:
[paste data here or write none]

Task:
1. Summarise the process in five lines: purpose, inputs, outputs, owners, records. Use only the procedure.
2. Risk areas: rank up to six areas of this process to audit, with the reason for each (past finding, KPI trend, change, complexity, impact on product or safety).
3. Questions: for each risk area, three to five open questions (How do you ... , Show me ... , What happens if ...). For each question give: the evidence to request (record, system screen, sample), what good looks like according to the procedure (short quote), and a trace sample suggestion (for example "pick three recent orders and follow them from input to record").
4. Interviews: questions by role (operator, supervisor, process owner) that test understanding and awareness, not memory.
5. Patterns to watch: gaps between procedure and practice, such as an outdated revision in use, records incomplete or signed late, training not evidenced, corrective actions closed without verification of effectiveness.
6. Time plan for the audit duration, with the most critical areas first.

Format: Tables for steps 2, 3 and 6. Questions must be short enough to be said aloud.

Rules: Do not quote clause numbers or requirement text from memory; refer to clauses only if I pasted the text, otherwise write [clause per our standard]. Do not state that something is a nonconformity. Do not invent KPI values, dates or findings. Questions must not point at individuals.
------------------------------------------------------------

WORKED EXAMPLE (all data invented for illustration)
Invented procedure: "Calibration control" in a fictional workshop. Summary of the input: all measuring devices are registered with an ID and due date; overdue devices are tagged and removed from use; calibration certificates are filed. Last audit: two hand tools found beyond their due date. KPI: 240 registered devices, 6 overdue at the last count. Recent change: new calibration management software introduced last quarter.

What a good answer contains:
- Calculation: 6 / 240 = 2.5 percent overdue, which Copilot may show because both numbers were given.
- Risk areas, ranked: (1) overdue devices still in use (past finding, KPI), (2) data migration into the new software (recent change), (3) action when a device is found out of tolerance (impact on product measured earlier).
- Questions for area 1: "Show me the list of devices due this month and pick three at the workstations." Evidence: the due-date list and the physical tag. Trace sample: three devices from the list, followed to their certificates.
- Questions for area 3: "What happens to parts measured with a device found out of tolerance?" Good looks like: as written in the procedure; Copilot quotes it if present or states that the procedure is silent, which is a finding candidate for the auditor to judge.
- Interview question for operators: "How do you know a gauge is still valid?" Time plan: 40 minutes area 1, 30 minutes area 2, 20 minutes area 3.

WHEN TO USE
When you plan a process audit and want a good question set quickly, when you audit an unfamiliar process, or when a new auditor needs a model of risk-based preparation. Also useful for supplier audits and for preparing for external audits by running a mock audit of the weakest process.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- The procedure or process description as text.
- The previous audit findings and open actions.
- KPIs, process changes, complaints or incidents.
- The time available and the roles you can interview.
- Optional: the standard's requirement text if you want clauses referenced.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A five-line process summary, ranked risk areas, questions with evidence to request and trace samples, role-based interview questions, patterns to watch and a time plan. The audit itself, evidence and findings are the auditor's work.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Reading the question list like a checklist. Follow evidence where it leads and use the list as a safety net.
- Letting Copilot cite clause numbers from memory. Paste the text or leave the clause open.
- Forgetting trace samples. Following three real examples finds more than ten theoretical questions.
- Asking closed yes or no questions. Use how, show me and what happens if.
- Auditing only the documents and not the workplace.

HOW TO ADAPT
For a supplier audit, replace roles with supplier roles and add "supplier controls of sub-tier suppliers". For an MRO process, add tasks such as tool control, parts traceability from receipt to installation and records completeness; keep the regulation-specific wording to what you paste. For layered process audits on the shop floor, ask for ten five-minute questions with expected answers. For follow-up audits, add the task "Check effectiveness of each corrective action: what evidence shows the cause is gone". For an audit programme, run the prompt for each process and ask for a combined year plan sorted by risk.

DATA PROTECTION AND LIMITS
Audit preparation includes findings and sometimes personal performance data. Do not paste audit reports with names of individuals; use roles. Interviews that evaluate individuals may need involvement of the works council and data protection officer according to local agreements. Customer-confidential or export-controlled documents should not be pasted unless your rules allow it. Nonconformities and their classification are determined by the auditor on evidence and recorded in your audit system, never by Copilot.

Where it runs: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, signed in with your work account. Paste the text or attach the file. With a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence Chat can also reach work content you are allowed to see; without it you supply the text yourself. Check in your tenant which applies. Microsoft Learn documents that prompts and responses in Copilot Chat with a work account fall under the Data Protection Addendum and are not used to train foundation models. Web search queries are handled separately (sent to Bing, outside that commitment), so ask your admin how web search is configured and keep confidential details out of prompts when it is on.
